title: Checkpoint: Cities
objective: After this level you can explain how streets, walls, parks and transport shape a city.
summary: Barcelona tore down its walls and Cerdà spread a chamfered grid, with gardens in each block, over the old field of fire. Speculators filled the gardens; Cerdà gave us the word urbanization.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale: the man who redrew Barcelona invented the word urbanization.
cards.body: Ildefons Cerdà is credited with coining it, in his General Theory of Urbanization (1867). His Barcelona pulls this whole chapter together: walls, grids, squares, gardens and traffic.

cards.headline: Walls down, grid out
cards.body: Barcelona's new district, the Eixample, was built on open land left clear to give a field of fire from the city walls. Level 83 showed walls cramping growing cities. In 1859, the engineer Ildefons Cerdà drew up a grid plan to extend Barcelona beyond its old walls, and it won royal approval. Level 82's grid, laid over the old killing ground.

cards.headline: Corners cut, gardens planned
cards.body: Cerdà cut the corners of his blocks at 45 degrees so traffic could see along the crossing streets. Every crossing became a small open space, a bit like Level 85's squares. His blocks were also meant to leave open space and gardens in the middle, Level 84's idea of green for everyone, tucked inside every block.

mascot.line: Look at Barcelona from above: all those clipped corners are Cerdà's.

cards.context: The plan was not fully carried out: within 30 years the open areas had been built over and building density tripled. Birkenhead's houses paid for its park; in Barcelona, the buildings won and the gardens lost. A plan is a promise, and every city decides how much of it to keep.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 complete
learned: What turns a settlement into a city, and why the first writing was bookkeeping.
Why so many cities are laid out on grids, and how torn-down walls became boulevards.
What makes streets and squares feel alive and safe, from places to sit to eyes on the street.
How new transport, from railways to highways, stretched cities out into suburbs.

questions.prompt: Why did Cerdà cut the corners of Barcelona's blocks at 45 degrees?

options.label: So traffic could see along the crossing streets
To save expensive stone on every corner building
options.rationale: The chamfers were about the crossings, not stone.

options.label: To follow the curved line of the old city walls
options.rationale: The walls were gone; the corners served traffic.

options.label: To copy the corners of Manhattan's 1811 grid

questions.explanation: Cerdà's chamfered corners gave traffic a view along the crossing streets, and turned each crossing into a small open space.

questions.prompt: What happened to the gardens planned inside the Eixample's blocks?

options.label: They became Barcelona's first public parks
They were built over; density tripled
They were dug out for a subway line
They are all still open gardens today
options.rationale: The plan wasn't carried out completely.

questions.explanation: Within 30 years the open areas were built over and building density tripled: the plan was not fully carried out.

questions.prompt: Cities recap: the Eixample was built on land once kept clear for the city walls. Why, as Level 83 showed, did walls like Barcelona's come down?

options.label: They were too beautiful to keep closed
They drew too many tourists into the old town
They cramped cities and blocked traffic
Kings needed their stone for new palaces
options.rationale: Level 83 points to crowding and traffic.

questions.explanation: As cities grew, walls caused overcrowding and poor sanitation and blocked traffic, so many came down; Barcelona's cleared land became the Eixample.

questions.prompt: Cities recap: the earliest tablets from Uruk were mostly what?

options.label: Poems about Gilgamesh
options.rationale: The epic was written down much later.

options.label: Maps of the city walls
Letters between kings
Lists and ledgers of goods

questions.explanation: The earliest Sumerian writing is Uruk's picture-sign tablets: ledgers of goods with numerals and names.

options.label: London's first underground line, opened 1863
options.rationale: That was the Metropolitan Railway itself, in 1863.

A children's theme park in New York's Central Park
A Paris district built on its demolished walls
